## The situation this solves

You have a model. It has parameters. You do not know most of them exactly — you
know roughly what each one could be, because somebody measured it once in a
different system, or estimated it from a figure, or nobody has ever measured it
at all.

So your prediction is not a number. It is a spread. Run the model across
everything you might plausibly believe and the answers come out wildly
different.

The question worth asking is not "what does the model predict?" It is:

> **Which of the numbers I don't know is responsible for the answers coming out
> so differently?**

That is all global sensitivity analysis is. Answer it and you know exactly which
measurement would be worth making — which is the most useful thing a model can
tell you before the fieldwork is done.

The worked example throughout is a winter tick–moose model with 13 uncertain
parameters, analysed over 50 years.

## Step 0. Why not just change one parameter at a time?

The instinct is to take your baseline parameter set, nudge one parameter by 10%,
see how much the answer moves, and repeat. This is **local** sensitivity, also
called OAT (one-at-a-time). Three things go wrong with it.

### It only describes one point

The derivative at your baseline tells you nothing about behaviour anywhere else.
Our model has an attachment probability that saturates at 1. Near saturation the
local sensitivity to the attachment rate $\beta_M$ is *exactly zero* — every tick
already finds a host, so making them better at finding hosts changes nothing.

Across its full plausible range, $\beta_M$ is the single most important parameter
in the model.

A local analysis run from a host-rich baseline would have reported "attachment
doesn't matter" and been completely wrong. Drag the baseline below to watch this
happen:

::: {.model-explorer}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lbeta0 = Inputs.range([-7.3, -4.7], {value: -5.0, step: 0.05,
  label: "Baseline log₁₀ β"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof hosts = Inputs.range([500, 6000], {value: 3000, step: 100,
  label: "Host abundance"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Schematic saturating attachment: P = 1 - exp(-beta * H * tau)
attach = (lb) => 1 - Math.exp(-Math.pow(10, lb) * hosts * 165)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
satCurve = {
  const out = [];
  for (let lb = -7.3; lb <= -4.7; lb += 0.02) out.push({lb: lb, P: attach(lb)});
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Local slope at the baseline, drawn as a short tangent segment
tangent = {
  const h = 0.02;
  const slope = (attach(lbeta0 + h) - attach(lbeta0 - h)) / (2 * h);
  const y0 = attach(lbeta0);
  return {
    slope: slope,
    seg: [{lb: lbeta0 - 0.5, P: y0 - 0.5 * slope},
          {lb: lbeta0 + 0.5, P: y0 + 0.5 * slope}]
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 340,
  marginLeft: 60,
  marginBottom: 45,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "log₁₀ attachment rate β →", grid: true, domain: [-7.3, -4.7]},
  y: {label: "↑ Attachment probability", grid: true, domain: [-0.05, 1.05]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(satCurve, {x: "lb", y: "P", fill: "#2c6e63", fillOpacity: 0.08}),
    Plot.line(satCurve, {x: "lb", y: "P", stroke: "#2c6e63", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.line(tangent.seg, {x: "lb", y: "P", stroke: "#c0563f",
      strokeWidth: 2.5, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot([{lb: lbeta0, P: attach(lbeta0)}], {x: "lb", y: "P",
      fill: "#c0563f", r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#999"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="margin:0.6rem 0 0 0; font-size:0.95rem;">
Local slope at this baseline: <b>${tangent.slope.toFixed(3)}</b> per decade of β.
Full range of the output across all plausible β: <b>${
  (Math.max(...satCurve.map(d => d.P)) - Math.min(...satCurve.map(d => d.P))).toFixed(3)
}</b>.
${tangent.slope < 0.02
  ? "<span style='color:#c0563f'><b>The local analysis says β is irrelevant. It is not.</b></span>"
  : "Here the baseline sits on the steep part, so local and global happen to agree."}
</p>`
```

:::

### It cannot see interactions

Holding everything else fixed means you never observe that $\beta_M$ behaves
differently depending on the aggregation parameter $k$. In our run the total
indices sum to about **2.4**, against 1.0 for a purely additive model — so most
of what the model is doing is interaction. OAT would have missed nearly all of
it.

### It explores almost nothing

With 13 parameters, moving along 13 axes out from a single point covers a
vanishingly small fraction of a 13-dimensional box.

**Global** sensitivity analysis instead varies *all* parameters *simultaneously*
across their *full plausible ranges*, and asks: of all the variation we see in
the output, how much is attributable to each input?

## Step 1. Understand what the answer will look like

Before any machinery, it is worth understanding what a variance decomposition
actually claims. It is simpler than the notation suggests, and you can see the
whole idea in four model runs.

Two parameters, each set Low or High. Four runs, four answers. **Drag the
answers and watch the split change:**

::: {.model-explorer}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof LL = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 1, step: 0.5, label: "β low, μ low"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof HL = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 9, step: 0.5, label: "β high, μ low"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof LH = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "β low, μ high"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof HH = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 18, step: 0.5, label: "β high, μ high"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sob = {
  const y = [LL, HL, LH, HH];
  const m = (LL + HL + LH + HH) / 4;
  const V = y.reduce((s, v) => s + (v - m) ** 2, 0) / 4;
  const bL = (LL + LH) / 2, bH = (HL + HH) / 2;
  const uL = (LL + HL) / 2, uH = (LH + HH) / 2;
  const Vb = ((bL - m) ** 2 + (bH - m) ** 2) / 2;
  const Vu = ((uL - m) ** 2 + (uH - m) ** 2) / 2;
  const Vs = Math.max(0, V - Vb - Vu);
  return {
    V: V, bL: bL, bH: bH, uL: uL, uH: uH,
    beta:   V > 0 ? Vb / V : 0,
    mu:     V > 0 ? Vu / V : 0,
    shared: V > 0 ? Vs / V : 0,
    effLo: HL - LL,
    effHi: HH - LH
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 150,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Share of the spread →", domain: [0, 1], grid: true,
      tickFormat: d => Math.round(d * 100) + "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {
    domain: ["β alone", "μ alone", "shared"],
    range: ["#2c6e63", "#7a9e6b", "#b9b4a8"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(
      [{p: "β alone", v: sob.beta}, {p: "μ alone", v: sob.mu},
       {p: "shared", v: sob.shared}],
      {x: "v", fill: "p", y: () => "", sort: null}
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0.9rem 0; font-size:0.95rem;">${
  sob.V === 0
    ? "All four answers are the same, so there is no spread to divide."
    : Math.abs(sob.effHi - sob.effLo) < 0.5
      ? `β lifts the answer by <b>${sob.effLo}</b> whether μ is low or high. Its
         effect does not depend on μ, so <b>the shared piece is zero</b> and the
         two totals add to exactly 1.`
      : `β lifts the answer by <b>${sob.effLo}</b> when μ is low, but by
         <b>${sob.effHi}</b> when μ is high. That inconsistency is the shared
         piece — it belongs to neither parameter on its own.`
}</p>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 190,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Total index →", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {
    domain: ["on its own", "via interaction"],
    range: ["#2c6e63", "#d6d2c6"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(
      [{p: "β", part: "on its own", v: sob.beta},
       {p: "β", part: "via interaction", v: sob.shared},
       {p: "μ", part: "on its own", v: sob.mu},
       {p: "μ", part: "via interaction", v: sob.shared}],
      {x: "v", y: "p", fill: "part", sort: null}
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0 0; font-size:0.95rem;">
Totals add to <b>${(sob.beta + sob.mu + 2 * sob.shared).toFixed(3)}</b>.
${sob.shared > 0.005
  ? "They exceed 1 because the shared piece is counted in both parameters' totals — it genuinely belongs to both."
  : "With no interaction, they add to exactly 1."}
</p>`
```

:::

At the default values the arithmetic is:

| $\beta$ | $\mu$ | answer |
|---|---|---|
| L | L | 1 |
| H | L | 9 |
| L | H | 2 |
| H | H | 18 |

Total spread (variance) = 46.25.

**$\beta$'s own piece.** Average when $\beta$ is low = 1.5, when high = 13.5. Far
apart, so $\beta$'s piece is 36.0 — that is **77.8%** of the spread.

**$\mu$'s own piece.** Average when low = 5.0, when high = 10.0. Closer, so
$\mu$'s piece is 6.25 — **13.5%**.

**Left over: 4.0, or 8.6%.** This is the shared piece, and here is why it exists:
$\beta$ lifts the answer by 8 when $\mu$ is low, but by 16 when $\mu$ is high.
$\beta$'s effect *depends on* $\mu$. That inconsistency cannot be credited to
either one alone, so it gets a piece of its own.

$$
77.8\% + 13.5\% + 8.6\% = 100\%
$$

Exactly. Nothing lost, nothing double counted. There is only one way to do this
split and it always adds up — that exactness is the point.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The one sentence to remember

*How much the average answer moves when you learn a parameter's value* is that
parameter's piece of the spread. We cannot rerun history with $\beta$ held fixed,
so instead we compare the average over every run where $\beta$ was low against
the average over every run where it was high.
:::

## Step 2. The formal version

That four-run split generalises. For a model $Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_p)$ with
**independent** inputs, the output variance decomposes uniquely:

$$
V(Y) = \sum_i V_i + \sum_{i<j} V_{ij} + \sum_{i<j<l} V_{ijl} + \dots + V_{12\dots p}
$$

- $V_i$ — variance explained by $X_i$ **on its own**
- $V_{ij}$ — the extra variance from $X_i$ and $X_j$ **acting together**, beyond
  their separate effects
- and so on for higher orders.

Divide through by $V(Y)$ and every term becomes a share summing to 1. This is the
**Sobol decomposition** — three plain words wearing a disguise. *Variance* is
just how spread out the answers are. *Decomposition* is cutting that spread into
pieces. *Sobol* is a person's name (Ilya Sobol, who worked it out) and carries no
meaning at all.

### The two indices you report

**First-order index**

$$
S_i = \frac{V_i}{V(Y)}
$$

The share of variance explained by $X_i$ alone. Equivalently: the fraction of
uncertainty you would eliminate by learning $X_i$ exactly.

**Total index**

$$
S_{T_i} = \frac{\sum_{\text{all terms containing } X_i} V_{\dots}}{V(Y)}
$$

$X_i$ alone *plus* everything it does through interactions. Equivalently: the
uncertainty that would remain if you learned every parameter *except* $X_i$.

Three diagnostics fall straight out:

| Reading | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $S_{T_i} - S_i$ | how much of this parameter's influence runs through interactions |
| $\sum_i S_i \approx 1$ | model is additive; parameters act independently |
| $\sum_i S_{T_i} \gg 1$ | strong interactions; the same variance is attributed to several parameters because it belongs to none of them alone |
| $S_{T_i} \approx 0$ | genuinely negligible — safe to fix and drop from the analysis |

Variance is the right currency because it is **model-free**: no assumption of
linearity, monotonicity or additivity. Compare a correlation coefficient, which
only sees monotonic trends. In our run $\mu_E$ showed a large Sobol index but a
near-zero Spearman correlation, because its effect is hump-shaped. A
correlation-based method would have declared it unimportant.

## Step 3. Choose the parameter ranges

This is the step with the least mathematics and by far the most consequence.

Every index is **conditional on the ranges**. A parameter given a wide range will
tend to look important; the same parameter pinned to a narrow range will look
irrelevant. This is not a flaw — it is correct behaviour, because the question
being asked is *"given what we don't know, what drives the uncertainty in our
prediction?"* A parameter you know precisely **should** rank low, even if the
model is mechanistically very sensitive to it.

What that meant in our case:

- `log10_beta_M` spans three decades because nobody has ever measured it. It came
  out top. That ranking is a statement about **our ignorance**, not purely about
  the biology.
- `lambda` spans ±40% because Drew & Samuel counted eggs directly. It ranked low
  partly because we know it well.
- `mu_E`'s two endpoints are the two competing readings of the same paper, so its
  index measures **what the unresolved argument costs us**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Always report the ranges next to the indices

An index without its range is not interpretable. A parameter can score low for
three completely different reasons — we know it well, it genuinely does nothing,
or it *cannot* do anything however wide the range. Those are three different
findings. Say which one you mean.
:::

Three practical rules that made the ranges defensible:

**Set ranges on the interpretable quantity, then invert.** We set the virulence
$\alpha_M$ by asking "how many ticks kill half a moose?" and solving

$$
\alpha = \frac{\ln 2}{\text{burden} \times \tau_A}
$$

Nobody can eyeball whether $2 \times 10^{-7}$ is sensible. Everybody can judge
38,000 ticks.

**Sample on a log scale when a range spans decades**, otherwise 90% of your draws
land in the top decade.

**Make ranges track the model's structure.** Our `beta_for()` helper derives
$\beta$'s range from the current host numbers, because what matters is
$\beta \times \text{hosts}$, never $\beta$ alone.

Where nothing is measured at all, bound it by something you do know. Winter tick
*is* established in Yukon, so $R_0 > 1$; it is at its northern range edge, so
$R_0$ is not enormous. We set $\beta_M$'s range to the values putting $R_0$
between roughly 1 and 70. Indirect, but a real constraint and far better than
three arbitrary decades.

```r
rng_dyn2 <- list(
  # beta_M: never measured. Bounded so R0 runs from ~1 to ~67.
  log10_beta_M  = c(-7.3, -4.7),

  # mu_E: egg + free-living larval mortality, from egg-to-questing
  # survival of 30% down to 2%:  mu_E = -log(survival) / tau_E
  mu_E          = c(0.01003, 0.03260),

  # mu_N: attached nymph mortality, nymph-to-adult survival 50% to 10%
  mu_N          = c(0.00420, 0.01396),

  lambda        = c(1500, 5000),      # eggs per surviving female

  # Stage durations: the climate levers. Arthropod development runs
  # 2-3x faster per 10 C, and Yukon is projected 4-6 C warmer.
  tau_E         = c(75, 180),
  tau_Q         = c(30, 120),
  tau_A         = c(140, 200),

  M0            = c(500, 6000),       # host abundance
  U0            = c(100, 6000),

  # alpha_M: set as the burden that kills half a moose, then inverted
  #   150,000 ticks -> log10 = -7.29  (tolerant)
  #     5,000 ticks -> log10 = -5.81  (vulnerable)
  log10_alpha_M = c(-7.29, -5.81),

  k             = c(0.02, 1.00),      # aggregation; small = more clumped
  rho_M         = c(1.00, 1.20),      # moose finite rate of increase
  rho_U         = c(1.00, 1.35)
)
```

## Step 4. Choose the design

You need parameter sets that cover the space efficiently. The options, with cost
for $p$ parameters:

| Design | Cost | Analysis it supports |
|---|---|---|
| Full factorial, $L$ levels | $L^p$ | ANOVA |
| Fractional factorial | $L^{p-k}$ | ANOVA |
| **eFAST (`fast99`)** | **$n \cdot p$** | **Fourier decomposition** |
| Sobol Monte Carlo | $n(p+2)$ | Sobol estimators |
| Morris | $r(p+1)$ | screening only — ranks, no quantities |
| Latin hypercube | $n$ | PRCC, regression — **not** ANOVA |

We used **eFAST**, for three reasons:

1. A full factorial at 3 levels samples each parameter at only three points. Our
   output spans about 10 orders of magnitude, and three points cannot describe a
   surface that curved. The curvature you miss gets misattributed as
   "interaction".
2. eFAST samples **continuously** along space-filling curves, so it handles
   nonlinearity properly.
3. Cost is **linear in the number of parameters**. Going from 7 to 13 parameters
   cost us 2,100 → 3,900 runs instead of 2,187 → 1.6 million.

### How eFAST samples

Every parameter gets its own **frequency**, and the design walks a single curve
through parameter space. As a scalar $s$ advances, each parameter oscillates:

$$
X_i(s) = G_i\big(\sin(\omega_i s)\big)
$$

where $\omega_i$ is parameter $i$'s distinct frequency and $G_i$ is the transform
making $X_i$ uniform over its range.

That sounds like a strange thing to do. Here is the trick: because each parameter
wiggles at a *different rate*, the model's answer wiggles back at that same rate.
Take the Fourier spectrum of the output, and the power sitting at parameter $i$'s
frequency is $V_i$. It is the same idea as picking one instrument out of a
recording because you know its pitch. No fitting, no guessing.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why LHS does not work with ANOVA

`multisensi`'s default engine is ANOVA, which needs each factor to take a few
*repeated* levels so there are residual degrees of freedom. A continuous Latin
hypercube gives every factor $n$ distinct values, the model is saturated, and the
decomposition fails. LHS is a perfectly good design — but pair it with PRCC or
regression, not ANOVA.
:::

## Step 5. Run the model

```r
run_design(X, years = 50, out_var = "M")
```

takes the design table and returns:

```
IN   3900 rows (parameter sets)  x  13 columns (parameters)
OUT  3900 rows (parameter sets)  x  51 columns (years)
```

Row $i$ out is the trajectory produced by row $i$ in. Note the output is
**multivariate** — 51 numbers per run, not one. That is what the next step is
for.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Analyse the log when the process is multiplicative

Our tick population is multiplicative — each year is last year times a growth
factor — so over 50 years small parameter differences compound into orders of
magnitude. On a raw scale the variance is then owned by the handful of runs that
exploded, no single parameter explains the level (because the level is a
*product* of all of them), first-order indices collapse to nearly zero, and
everything piles into interaction.

Taking logs turns that product into a sum, which is exactly the additive
structure a variance decomposition is built for, and the main effects reappear.
Host populations vary far less, so they don't need it.
:::

## Step 6. Reduce the output with PCA

We have 51 outputs, one per year. We could run 51 separate sensitivity analyses
and get 51 sets of indices. Two reasons not to:

1. **It is unreadable.** 13 parameters × 51 years × 2 index types = 1,326
   numbers. There is no ranking in there a person can act on.
2. **The outputs are massively redundant.** Year 30 and year 31 are almost the
   same number. Naively averaging 51 sets of indices would count the same
   information dozens of times over.

PCA finds a small set of **orthogonal shapes** that trajectories vary along.
Instead of 51 correlated numbers per run, each run is described by a handful of
uncorrelated component scores. In our run:

| Component | Variance explained | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| PC1 | 75.4% | the overall **level** — how high or low the herd sits |
| PC2 | 14.2% | the **transient shape** — early crash and partial recovery |
| PC3 | 3.8% | early oscillation |
| PC4 | 2.6% | negligible |

Three components carry **93.4%** of everything that varies between trajectories.

### Why orthogonality is the whole point

This is the part usually glossed over, and it is the reason the PCA is there at
all. PCA components are **uncorrelated by construction**, which means the total
variance splits *additively* across them:

$$
V(\text{trajectories}) = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 + \dots
$$

Because there is no overlap between components, you may analyse each one
separately and then combine the results by a weighted sum **without double
counting**. If the components were correlated — as the 51 yearly outputs are —
that combination step would be invalid.

So the PCA is not cosmetic dimension reduction. It is what makes Step 8
mathematically legitimate.

There is an interpretation bonus too. Each component has a temporal loading
profile showing how it weights each year, so you are no longer decomposing
variance "at year 37" — you are decomposing variance in **trajectory shape**.
Asking which parameters drive the overall level, and which drive the transient,
is a better question than asking about any single year.

## Step 7. Decompose the variance

Each component's scores are one number per run, so this is now an ordinary scalar
problem. eFAST estimates the decomposition from the Fourier spectrum:

| Index | How it is read off the spectrum | Plain English |
|---|---|---|
| $S_i$ | power at $\omega_i$ and its harmonics | learn this one number and this much guesswork goes away |
| $S_{T_i}$ | $1 - V_{\sim i}/V$: everything except the *other* parameters' frequencies | learn all the others but not this one, and this much guesswork is left |

Because it reads variance off a spectrum rather than fitting a model, there is
**no residual term**. Nothing is left over.

## Step 8. Aggregate to one number per parameter

Steps 6 and 7 give indices *per component*. To get one number per parameter, use
the **Generalised Sensitivity Index** (Lamboni et al.) — the inertia-weighted
average:

$$
\text{GSI}_i = \frac{\sum_c \lambda_c \, S_{ic}}{\sum_c \lambda_c}
$$

where $S_{ic}$ is the index of parameter $i$ on component $c$ and $\lambda_c$ is
that component's eigenvalue. Components are weighted by how much trajectory
variation they actually explain, so PC1 at 75.4% dominates and PC3 at 3.8% barely
contributes.

**This weighted sum is only valid because the components are orthogonal.** That
is the payoff from Step 6. Averaging the 51 raw yearly indices instead would count
the same information dozens of times over.

## The whole thing in R

```r
library(multisensi)

gsa_time <- multisensi(
  design        = fast99,               # 1. how the sample is built
  model         = run_design,           # 2. run the model on every row
  reduction     = basis.ACP,            # 3. PCA the 51 yearly outputs
  scale         = FALSE,                #    covariance, not correlation
  design.args   = list(
    factors = names(parameters_range),
    n       = 1000,                     # runs per parameter
    q       = "qunif",
    q.arg   = lapply(parameters_range,
                     function(r) list(min = r[1], max = r[2]))
  ),
  analysis      = analysis.sensitivity, # 4. decompose the variance
  analysis.args = list(keep.outputs = FALSE)
)

summary(gsa_time)
```

What comes back:

| Object | Contents |
|---|---|
| `gsa$L` | loadings — the shape over time of each component, length 51 |
| `gsa$H` | scores — one per run, how strongly that run shows the shape |
| `gsa$lambda` | eigenvalues, the variance of each component |
| `gsa$mSI` | first-order indices $S_i$ |
| `gsa$tSI` | total indices $S_{T_i}$ |

`scale = FALSE` means PCA on the **covariance**, not the correlation matrix. That
is correct here because all 51 columns are the same quantity in the same units —
standardising would give a quiet year the same weight as a year of collapse.

::: {.callout-important}
## `design = fast99` means this is *not* ANOVA

`design = fast99` with `analysis = analysis.sensitivity` is the eFAST route.
ANOVA (`analysis.anoasg`) is the other engine, used when you pass discrete levels
through `design.args` instead of ranges. They estimate the same quantity by
different means — see the comparison at the end.
:::

## Reading the results

Our run, watching the moose herd:

| Parameter | $S_i$ (alone) | $S_{T_i}$ (total) | via interactions |
|---|---|---|---|
| `log10_beta_M` | 0.31 | **0.80** | 61% |
| `mu_E` | 0.10 | 0.42 | 76% |
| `k` | 0.26 | 0.41 | 37% |
| `rho_M` | 0.03 | 0.27 | 89% |
| `lambda` | 0.01 | 0.17 | 94% |
| `log10_alpha_M` | 0.005 | 0.16 | 97% |
| `rho_U` | 0.03 | 0.16 | 81% |

**Totals sum to about 2.4, not 1.** The model is strongly non-additive. The
practical consequence is blunt: *"increasing X does Y to moose" is not a sentence
this model supports* without stating what the other parameters are doing. Any
single-parameter policy claim needs a caveat.

**A big gap between $S_i$ and $S_{T_i}$ means context-dependent.**
`log10_alpha_M` has a first-order index of 0.005 and a total of 0.16 — on its own
it does essentially nothing, but it matters in combination. Virulence only bites
once attachment has already put enough ticks on the animal.

**A small gap means the parameter acts independently.** `k` at 0.26 / 0.41 has
the most autonomous effect in the model.

**Indices are unsigned.** They tell you *how much*, never *which way*. Direction
has to come from somewhere else — a scatter of output against each parameter, or
PRCC on a random or LHS sample. This matters: `rho_U` turned out **negative**
(more alternative hosts → fewer moose), which no sensitivity index would have
told us.

### What to do with the answer

1. **Measure the top-ranked uncertain parameter.** `beta_M` at 0.80 total, with
   no empirical basis at all. That is the highest-value fieldwork in the system.
2. **Settle cheap disputes.** `mu_E` at 0.42 comes down to one sentence in a 1986
   paper.
3. **Fix and forget the negligible ones.** Anything with $S_{T_i} \approx 0$ can
   be pinned at its baseline in future work.
4. **Report ranges alongside indices. Always.**

## Pitfalls

**Indices are conditional on the ranges.** `beta_M` was allowed three decades;
`rho_M` was allowed 12%. Some of beta's dominance is that, and you must say so.

**eFAST assumes independent inputs.** We have a live violation: `mu_E` and `mu_N`
are the same disputed reading of the same paper. If one value is right, the other
almost certainly is too — so the sweep explores combinations that cannot both be
true, while the indices are computed as though the two are independent. State
this in the methods rather than hoping nobody notices.

**eFAST cannot warn you when it fails.** It has no residual by construction. If
$n$ is too small or frequencies interfere, you get plausible-looking numbers with
no signal that anything went wrong. ANOVA's residual is a *feature* — a built-in
confession that "27% of this I could not explain".

The trade-off runs opposite to intuition:

| | eFAST | ANOVA |
|---|---|---|
| Functional form | agnostic | limited by grid and formula order |
| Cost | $n \cdot p$ | $L^p$ |
| **Warns you when it fails** | **no** | **yes — the residual** |

Both engines estimate the *same* Sobol decomposition. They differ in the
estimator, not the target. Which is the argument for running both on a small
subset once and checking they agree:

```r
top6 <- c("log10_beta_M", "mu_E", "k", "rho_M", "lambda", "log10_alpha_M")
a <- run_gsa_dyn(as_levels(rng_dyn2[top6]))   # ANOVA, has a residual
b <- run_gsa_dyn(rng_dyn2[top6])              # eFAST, does not
plot_gsi(a); plot_gsi(b)                      # same ranking?
```

**Watch for near-zero variance.** Indices summing above 1 in the early years of
our run were exactly this: tiny variance plus a finite sample gives noisy
estimates.

**Different questions need different analyses.** $R_0$ cannot rank `alpha_M`,
`k`, `rho_M` or `rho_U` — they do not appear in it, because $R_0$ is a
low-density quantity. Establishment and host collapse are different questions.

## Further reading

- Saltelli, A. et al. (2008). *Global Sensitivity Analysis: The Primer.* The
  standard reference.
- Lamboni, M., Monod, H. & Makowski, D. (2011). Multivariate sensitivity analysis
  to measure global contribution of input factors in dynamic models.
  *Reliability Engineering & System Safety.* The GSI.
- Marino, S. et al. (2008). A methodology for performing global uncertainty and
  sensitivity analysis in systems biology. *Journal of Theoretical Biology.* The
  LHS/PRCC route, widely used in epidemiology.
- The `multisensi`, `sensitivity` and `sensobol` R packages.
